FFIRE — Software Requirements Specification | Page 4
1.1 Purpose
This Software Requirements Specification (SRS) defines the functional, non-functional, and architectural
requirements  for  the  Financial  Fraud  Investigation  Reasoning  Engine  (FFIRE) —  a  multi-step,
explainable reasoning platform that investigates suspicious financial transactions using a deterministic
LangGraph-based  execution  pipeline,  structured  data  retrieval,  and  Large  Language  Model  (LLM)
reasoning grounded in verifiable evidence. This document is intended for engineering teams, architects,
QA, compliance stakeholders, and reviewers who require a precise, unambiguous specification of system
behaviour.
1.2 Scope
FFIRE  investigates  individual  flagged  transactions  and  produces  a  fully  traceable,  evidence-backed
investigation report explaining  why a transaction is suspicious — rather than emitting an opaque risk
score.  The  system  decomposes  an  investigation  into  discrete  reasoning  tasks  (customer  history,
merchant reputation, device fingerprint, geolocation, transaction velocity, and historical fraud cases),
retrieves supporting evidence from structured and unstructured data sources, applies a hybrid rule-based
and LLM-based risk reasoning layer, validates conclusions against guardrails to prevent hallucination, and
produces a final report suitable for compliance audit and human review.
In Scope
Transaction-level fraud investigation, evidence retrieval orchestration, explainable risk reasoning, retry and
escalation logic, audit logging, REST API, investigator dashboard.
Out of Scope
Real-time transaction blocking, core banking ledger modification, payment processing, and regulatory filing
automation (e.g. SAR submission) are out of scope for this release; the engine produces recommendations
only.
Introduction
C H A P T E R  0 1
FFIRE — Software Requirements Specification | Page 5
1.3 Objectives
Explainability
Every conclusion must be traceable to retrieved
evidence — no unsupported claims are permitted in
a final report.
Determinism
Identical inputs must always traverse the same
execution graph, ensuring reproducible, auditable
investigations.
Resilience
Transient retrieval failures must be retried
automatically before escalating to human review.
Auditability
Every state transition, tool call, and evidence
reference is logged for compliance review.
1.4 Background
Traditional fraud detection systems rely on supervised machine learning models or static rule engines that
output a binary flag or a numeric risk score with little to no explanation. Investigators must then manually
reconstruct the supporting evidence — a process that can take hours per case. FFIRE inverts this model:
instead of predicting fraud and asking a human to justify it, the system performs the investigation itself, in
the  same  structured  manner  a  human  financial  crime  analyst  would,  and  presents  the  supporting
evidence alongside the conclusion.
1.5 Existing Problems
Problem Impact
Black-box ML risk scores Analysts cannot justify decisions to regulators or customers
High false-positive rates Wasted investigator hours, customer friction
Free-form LLM chat agents Inconsistent reasoning paths, hallucinated conclusions
Manual evidence gathering Investigations take hours instead of seconds
No audit trail of reasoning Difficult to pass regulatory and internal audit review
1.6 Proposed Solution
FFIRE implements the investigation as an explicit, inspectable LangGraph state machine. Each node
performs  one  well-defined  responsibility  (planning,  retrieval,  comparison,  reasoning,  validation)  and
updates a shared, strongly-typed state object. Guardrail nodes enforce that every claim in the final report
is grounded in retrieved evidence, and a confidence-based routing mechanism escalates uncertain cases
to human review rather than guessing.
1.7 Expected Benefits
Investigation turnaround reduced from hours to seconds for routine cases.
Every conclusion is fully traceable to source evidence, satisfying audit and regulatory requirements.
Deterministic execution graph enables reliable testing, monitoring, and continuous improvement.
• 
• 
• 
FFIRE — Software Requirements Specification | Page 6
Human-in-the-loop escalation preserves analyst oversight for high-risk or ambiguous cases.• 
FFIRE — Software Requirements Specification | Page 7
2.1 Rule-Based Fraud Detection
Early fraud detection systems relied on hand-crafted rules (e.g. transaction amount thresholds, velocity
limits). These systems are interpretable but brittle — they cannot adapt to novel fraud patterns and
generate high false-positive rates as fraud tactics evolve.
2.2 Machine Learning Approaches
Supervised models (gradient boosted trees, neural networks) trained on historical labelled fraud data
improve detection accuracy but sacrifice interpretability. Post-hoc explanation methods (SHAP , LIME)
approximate feature importance but do not constitute a verifiable, evidence-grounded explanation.
2.3 Explainable AI (XAI)
Explainable AI research emphasizes that high-stakes financial decisions require explanations that are
faithful to the underlying decision process, not merely plausible-sounding narratives. FFIRE addresses
this by constraining the LLM reasoning layer to cite only retrieved, verifiable evidence.
2.4 Multi-Agent and Graph-Orchestrated Systems
Recent advances in agentic AI frameworks (LangGraph, AutoGen, CrewAI) allow developers to define
explicit  execution  graphs  rather  than  relying  on  free-form  agent  loops.  This  provides  control  over
reasoning  order,  supports  retries  and  conditional  branching,  and  produces  deterministic,  auditable
execution traces.
2.5 Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
RAG grounds LLM outputs in retrieved documents rather than parametric memory, substantially reducing
hallucination. FFIRE extends this concept beyond document retrieval to structured database queries, API
calls, and historical case retrieval from a vector knowledge base.
2.6 Enterprise AI Requirements
Enterprise deployments — particularly in regulated industries such as banking — demand reproducibility,
audit trails, role-based access control, and human oversight. These requirements directly shape FFIRE's
architecture, as detailed in subsequent chapters.
Literature Review
C H A P T E R  0 2
FFIRE — Software Requirements Specification | Page 8
3.1 Statement
Existing  financial  fraud  detection  systems  output  risk  scores  or  binary  flags  without  a  transparent,
verifiable chain of reasoning, forcing human investigators to manually reconstruct evidence. Free-form
conversational AI agents, while more flexible, lack deterministic execution and are prone to hallucinated or
unsupported conclusions — both unacceptable in a regulated financial environment.
3.2 Why Current Systems Fail
Failure Mode Description
False Positives Static rule thresholds flag legitimate transactions, eroding investigator trust and customer
experience.
Hallucination Free-form LLM agents may fabricate plausible-sounding but unverified explanations.
No Explainability ML risk scores cannot be traced back to specific evidentiary facts required for compliance
review.
No Investigation
Workflow
Systems flag transactions but do not perform the multi-step investigation a human analyst
would.
3.3 Design Implication
FFIRE must combine the flexibility of LLM reasoning with the determinism, auditability, and grounding
guarantees of a structured workflow engine — the central architectural decision explored in Chapters 5–9.
Problem Statement
C H A P T E R  0 3
FFIRE — Software Requirements Specification | Page 9
4.1 Functional Objectives
FO-1: Accept an investigation request for a transaction or customer identifier.
FO-2: Decompose the investigation into discrete, ordered reasoning tasks.
FO-3: Retrieve customer, transaction, merchant, device, and location evidence in parallel.
FO-4: Compare retrieved evidence against historical fraud patterns in the knowledge base.
FO-5: Compute a combined risk score using rule-based and LLM-based reasoning.
FO-6: Validate that every claim in the generated report is grounded in retrieved evidence.
FO-7: Retry failed retrieval or validation steps up to a configurable threshold.
FO-8: Escalate to human review when confidence falls below a configurable threshold.
FO-9: Generate a final, structured, human-readable investigation report.
FO-10: Log every node execution, tool call, and decision for audit purposes.
4.2 Non-Functional Objectives
Category Requirement
Performance P95 investigation latency < 8 seconds for standard-complexity cases.
Availability 99.9% uptime for the API gateway and orchestration layer.
Scalability Support horizontal scaling of retrieval and reasoning workers via Kubernetes.
Security All PII encrypted at rest (AES-256) and in transit (TLS 1.2+).
Auditability Every investigation must produce an immutable, timestamped audit trail.
Explainability 100% of generated claims must cite a specific evidence source.
Maintainability Graph nodes must be independently testable and replaceable.
4.3 Business Objectives
Reduce average fraud investigation time by at least 80%.
Reduce false-positive escalations to human analysts by at least 30%.
Provide audit-ready documentation for every automated decision.
4.4 Research Objectives
Evaluate deterministic graph-based orchestration against free-form agentic reasoning for grounding
quality.

5.1 Architectural Overview
FFIRE follows a layered architecture: a presentation layer (investigator dashboard), an API gateway, a
LangGraph orchestration layer, a retrieval layer spanning structured and unstructured data sources, and a
reasoning/validation layer that produces the final explainable report.
Figure 5.1 — FFIRE High-Level System Architecture
5.2 Layer Responsibilities
Layer Responsibility
API Gateway Authentication, request validation, rate limiting, routing to orchestrator.
LangGraph OrchestratorExecutes the deterministic investigation state machine.
Retrieval Layer Queries PostgreSQL ledger, vector knowledge base, and external KYC/AML APIs.
Reasoning Layer Combines rule engine output with LLM-based grounded reasoning.

FFIRE — Software Requirements Specification | Page 13
6.1 Execution Graph
The  investigation  is  modelled  as  an  explicit  directed  graph  of  nodes,  each  performing  a  single
responsibility and reading/writing a shared state object. The graph guarantees that the AI cannot skip
steps or reorder reasoning arbitrarily.
LangGraph Execution Graph
C H A P T E R  0 6
FFIRE — Software Requirements Specification | Page 14
Figure 6.1 — FFIRE LangGraph Execution Pipeline
START
Planner — Decompose Investigation Tasks
Parallel Retrieval — Customer / Transaction / Merchant / Device
Velocity & Location Analysis
Knowledge Base Lookup (Past Fraud Cases)
Risk Reasoning (LLM + Rule Engine)
Evidence Verification (Guardrails)
Retry? — on failure / low confidence
Human Review (if confidence < threshold)
Generate Explainable Investigation Report
END
FFIRE — Software Requirements Specification | Page 15
6.2 Shared State Object
state = {
    "transaction_id": "T-78491",
    "tasks": [],
    "customer_evidence": {},
    "transaction_evidence": {},
    "merchant_evidence": {},
    "device_evidence": {},
    "location_evidence": {},
    "historical_cases": [],
    "risk_score": None,
    "confidence": None,
    "validated": False,
    "retry_count": 0,
    "report": None
}
6.3 Node Definitions (LangGraph)
graph.add_node("planner", planner_node)
graph.add_node("retrieve_customer", retrieve_customer_node)
graph.add_node("retrieve_transaction", retrieve_transaction_node)
graph.add_node("retrieve_merchant", retrieve_merchant_node)
graph.add_node("retrieve_device", retrieve_device_node)
graph.add_node("velocity_check", velocity_node)
graph.add_node("knowledge_lookup", knowledge_node)
graph.add_node("risk_reasoning", reasoning_node)
graph.add_node("validator", validator_node)
graph.add_node("human_review", human_review_node)
graph.add_node("report_generator", report_node)
FFIRE — Software Requirements Specification | Page 16
7.1 Planner Module
Decomposes the incoming investigation request into an ordered list of evidence-gathering and analysis
tasks based on the transaction type and available data sources.
7.2 Retriever Modules
Module Data Source Output
Customer Retriever PostgreSQL — customer_profileKYC status, account age, risk tier
Transaction Retriever PostgreSQL — transactions Amount, timestamp, channel, status
Merchant Retriever PostgreSQL / External API Merchant category, historical fraud rate
Device Retriever Device fingerprint service Device ID, OS, first-seen date
Location Retriever Geo-IP / GPS service Country, distance from home location
7.3 Tool Executor
A unified interface that wraps all external tool calls (database queries, API calls, vector search) with
timeout handling, retry logic, and structured error reporting back into the shared state object.
7.4 Fraud Analyzer
Applies a hybrid rule engine (velocity limits, geolocation mismatch, device-change heuristics) combined
with LLM-based pattern reasoning over the aggregated evidence.
7.5 Knowledge Retriever
Performs a similarity search over a vector database of previously confirmed fraud cases to surface
analogous historical patterns relevant to the current investigation.
7.6 Evidence Collector
Aggregates outputs from all retriever modules into a normalized evidence bundle consumed by the
reasoning engine.
7.7 Reasoning Engine
Constructs a grounded prompt containing only retrieved evidence (no free recall) and instructs the LLM to
produce a structured risk explanation with explicit citations to evidence fields.
Detailed Module Design
C H A P T E R  0 7
FFIRE — Software Requirements Specification | Page 17
7.8 Validator
Parses the LLM output and verifies that every factual claim references a field present in the evidence
bundle; unsupported claims trigger a retry or escalation.
7.9 Confidence Calculator
Combines rule-engine score, LLM self-reported confidence, and evidence completeness into a single
normalized confidence value used for routing decisions.
7.10 Audit Logger
Persists every node execution, input/output state delta, tool call, and timing metric to an immutable audit
log table for compliance review.
7.11 Human Review Module
Pauses graph execution and surfaces the case, evidence, and draft explanation to a human analyst when
confidence is below threshold or a high-risk action is detected.

8.3 DFD Level 2 — Risk Analysis Process (Narrative)
Process 3.0 (Risk Analysis) further decomposes into: 3.1 Velocity Check, 3.2 Geolocation Comparison,
3.3 Device Trust Scoring, 3.4 Merchant Risk Lookup, and 3.5 Historical Pattern Matching against the
fraud knowledge base. Each sub-process reads from the evidence bundle produced in Level 1 and writes
a partial risk signal that is aggregated by the Confidence Calculator before reasoning proceeds.

investigation_id UUID FOREIGN KEY, INDEXED
action VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL
10.2 Indexing Strategy
Composite index on (account_id, timestamp) for transaction velocity queries.
B-tree index on investigation.status for dashboard filtering.
HNSW vector index on the fraud knowledge base embedding column for similarity search.

submission through to the delivery of the final explainable report.
Figure 11.1 — Sequence Diagram: End-to-End Fraud Investigation
11.2 Retry Sequence (Narrative)
When the Retrieval Layer raises a timeout exception, the Orchestrator catches the failure, increments
state.retry_count, and re-invokes the failed retrieval node up to a configured maximum (default 3). If
retries are exhausted, the Orchestrator routes execution to the Human Review node rather than producing
an unsubstantiated report.

13.1 LangGraph States
The investigation pipeline is implemented as a finite state machine. Transitions are deterministic except
for two conditional branches: retry-on-failure and confidence-based human escalation.
State Machine Diagram
C H A P T E R  1 3
FFIRE — Software Requirements Specification | Page 27
Figure 13.1 — FFIRE State Machine Diagram
13.2 Transition Rules
From State To State Condition
START
Planning
Retrieving Customer Data
Retrieving Transaction Data
Retrieving Merchant & Device Data
Analyzing Risk
Validating Evidence
Retry (on failure)
Human Review (low confidence)
Generating Report
END
FFIRE — Software Requirements Specification | Page 28
Validating EvidenceRetry retrieval failure OR ungrounded claim detected
Validating EvidenceGenerating Report all claims grounded AND confidence ≥ threshold
Validating EvidenceHuman Review confidence < threshold after max retries
Retry Retrieving Customer/Transaction Dataretry_count < max_retries
Retry Human Review retry_count ≥ max_retries

14.2 Decision Points
The single decision diamond in the activity flow ("Confidence ≥ Threshold?") determines whether the
system proceeds directly to report generation or routes to the retry/human-review sub-flow described in
Chapter 13.

16.1 Deployment Topology
Figure 16.1 — FFIRE Deployment Diagram
16.2 Scaling Strategy
API Gateway and LangGraph Worker pods scale horizontally based on request queue depth.
PostgreSQL uses a managed read-replica configuration for retrieval-heavy workloads.
Redis provides session caching and serves as the message bus for asynchronous retry scheduling.
Monitoring stack tracks node latency, retry counts, and confidence-score distributions in real time.

FFIRE — Software Requirements Specification | Page 33
17.1 Access Control
FFIRE  implements  Role-Based  Access  Control  (RBAC)  with  three  primary  roles:  Fraud  Analyst,
Administrator, and Compliance Officer, each scoped to a distinct set of permitted operations.
17.2 Authentication
All API access requires a signed JWT issued by the identity provider, validated on every request at the
API Gateway layer with a maximum token lifetime of 15 minutes and refresh-token rotation.
17.3 Data Protection
Encryption at Rest
AES-256 for all PII and transaction data in
PostgreSQL.
Encryption in Transit
TLS 1.2+ enforced for all internal and external traffic.
PII Minimization
Only fields required for the current reasoning step
are passed into LLM prompts.
Secrets Management
API keys and database credentials stored in a
managed secrets vault, never in source control.
17.4 LLM-Specific Guardrails
Prompt injection defense: retrieved evidence is sanitized and clearly delimited from system
instructions.
Output schema validation: LLM responses must conform to a strict JSON schema before being
accepted.
Rate limiting on LLM and tool invocations to prevent runaway loops.
17.5 Audit and Compliance
Every investigation produces an immutable audit record, retained per regulatory data-retention policy, and
exportable for examiner review.

18.1 Reasoning Pipeline
Figure 18.1 — Reasoning Strategy Pipeline
18.2 Role of Each Stage

Reasoning Strategy
C H A P T E R  1 8

Verifier

FFIRE — Software Requirements Specification | Page 35
Planner Determines which evidence categories are relevant to the case type.
Decomposer Breaks the investigation into independently executable sub-tasks.
Retriever Executes data retrieval tools against structured and vector sources.
Verifier Confirms evidence completeness before reasoning begins.
Reasoner Generates a grounded risk explanation referencing specific evidence fields.
Critic Reviews the reasoner's draft for unsupported claims or logical gaps.
Validator Performs final grounding checks and computes the confidence score.
Reporter Formats the final, citation-annotated investigation report.
FFIRE — Software Requirements Specification | Page 36
19.1 Planner Prompt (Template)
You are a financial fraud investigation planner. Given the transaction summary below,
output a JSON list of evidence-gathering tasks required to investigate it. Only select tasks
from the approved task catalog: [customer_history, transaction_detail, merchant_reputation,
device_fingerprint, location_check, velocity_check, historical_fraud_match].
Transaction: {{transaction_summary}}
19.2 Reasoner Prompt (Template)
You are a fraud investigation reasoning engine. Using ONLY the evidence provided below,
explain whether this transaction is likely fraudulent. Every claim must reference a specific
evidence field by name. If evidence is insufficient to support a conclusion, state this 
explicitly
rather than guessing.
Evidence: {{evidence_bundle}}
19.3 Validator Prompt (Template)
Review the draft explanation below against the evidence bundle. Flag any sentence that
is not directly supported by a named evidence field. Output a list of unsupported claims, or 
an
empty list if all claims are grounded.
Draft: {{draft_explanation}}
Evidence: {{evidence_bundle}}
19.4 Report Prompt (Template)
Format the validated explanation as a structured investigation report with sections:
Summary, Evidence Table, Risk Factors, Confidence Score, and Recommendation. Use only the
validated, grounded content provided.
Prompt Engineering
C H A P T E R  1 9
FFIRE — Software Requirements Specification | Page 37
20.1 Guardrail Principles
Grounding
Every claim must cite a specific evidence field;
ungrounded claims are rejected before reaching the
report.
Source Verification
Evidence must originate from an authenticated
retrieval tool call, never from LLM free recall.
Confidence Threshold
Reports are only finalized automatically when
confidence ≥ 0.85 (configurable).
Retry
Transient failures trigger automatic retry up to 3
attempts before escalation.
Escalation
Low-confidence or high-risk cases are routed to
human review rather than auto-finalized.
Hallucination Detection
A dedicated Critic node cross-checks every
sentence of the draft explanation against the
evidence bundle.
20.2 Guardrail Enforcement Flow
The Validator node parses the Reasoner's draft output, extracts each factual claim, and checks it against
the evidence bundle's field names and values. Any claim that cannot be matched to a specific evidence
field is flagged; if any flagged claim exists, the graph transitions to the Retry state rather than producing a
final report, ensuring the system fails closed rather than open.
Guardrails
C H A P T E R  2 0
FFIRE — Software Requirements Specification | Page 38
21.1 Composite Risk Model
FFIRE computes a composite risk score combining three independent signals, weighted and normalized
to a 0–100 scale.
Signal Weight Source
Rule Engine Score 35% Velocity limits, geolocation mismatch, device-change heuristics
LLM Reasoning Score 40% Grounded explanation confidence from the Reasoner/Critic stages
Historical Pattern Match25% Vector similarity to confirmed historical fraud cases
21.2 Risk Tiers
Score Range Tier Action
0–39 Low Auto-clear, log only
40–69 Medium Auto-generate report, periodic analyst review
70–100 High Mandatory human review before disposition
Risk Scoring
C H A P T E R  2 1
FFIRE — Software Requirements Specification | Page 39
22.1 Create Investigation
POST /api/v1/investigations
{
  "transaction_id": "T-78491",
  "priority": "standard"
}
Response 202 Accepted
{
  "investigation_id": "INV-20260630-0091",
  "status": "PROCESSING"
}
22.2 Get Investigation Report
GET /api/v1/investigations/{investigation_id}
Response 200 OK
{
  "investigation_id": "INV-20260630-0091",
  "status": "COMPLETED",
  "risk_score": 82,
  "confidence": 0.91,
  "summary": "Transaction flagged due to new device, location mismatch...",
  "evidence": [
    {"field": "device.first_seen", "value": "2026-06-30"},
    {"field": "location.country_diff", "value": true}
  ]
}
22.3 Error Codes
Code Meaning
400 Invalid or malformed transaction identifier
404 Investigation or transaction not found
409 Investigation already in progress for this transaction
422 Insufficient evidence to complete investigation automatically
503 Upstream retrieval or LLM provider unavailable

FFIRE — Software Requirements Specification | Page 40
23.1 Dashboard Overview
The investigator dashboard surfaces a queue of pending and completed investigations, filterable by risk
tier, status, and assigned analyst.
23.2 Key Screens
Screen Purpose
Transaction Search Locate a transaction or customer to initiate an investigation.
Fraud Timeline Chronological view of evidence events leading up to the flagged transaction.
Evidence Panel Inspect raw evidence records underlying each cited claim.
Reasoning Graph ViewVisualize the LangGraph execution trace for the current investigation.
Investigation Report Final, citation-annotated explanation with risk tier and recommendation.
Frontend Design
C H A P T E R  2 3
FFIRE — Software Requirements Specification | Page 41
Real-Time Streaming: Move from on-demand investigation to continuous streaming risk assessment
as transactions occur.
Graph Database Integration: Model customer-merchant-device relationships as a graph for advanced
ring-fraud detection.
Cross-Bank Fraud Intelligence: Federated sharing of anonymized fraud patterns across institutions.
Multi-Agent Collaboration: Specialized sub-agents for card fraud, wire fraud, and account-takeover
investigations operating under a shared orchestration layer.
Federated Learning: Improve the rule and embedding models using decentralized training across
participating institutions without sharing raw customer data.
Voice Investigator Interface: Conversational access to investigation reports for field analysts.
Future Scope
C H A P T E R  2 4
• 
• 
• 
• 
• 
• 
FFIRE — Software Requirements Specification | Page 42
FFIRE demonstrates that financial fraud investigation can be automated without sacrificing explainability,
determinism, or auditability — the three properties most critical to regulated financial environments. By
modelling the investigation as an explicit LangGraph state machine with strict grounding guardrails, retry
logic,  and  confidence-based  human  escalation,  the  system  delivers  investigation-grade  explanations
rather than opaque risk scores. This architecture generalizes beyond fraud investigation to any enterprise
domain  requiring  auditable,  multi-step  AI  reasoning  —  including  IT  incident  root-cause  analysis,
manufacturing defect investigation, and regulatory compliance review — positioning FFIRE as a reusable
reasoning platform rather than a single-purpose application.
Conclusion
C H A P T E R  2 5
FFIRE — Software Requirements Specification | Page 43
A.1 Glossary
LangGraph
A library for building stateful, multi-step LLM applications as explicit execution graphs.
Grounding
The property that every generated claim is traceable to a specific piece of retrieved evidence.
RAG
Retrieval-Augmented Generation — supplementing LLM context with retrieved external data.
Guardrail
A validation mechanism that prevents the system from producing unsupported or unsafe output.
KYC
Know Your Customer — identity verification processes required of financial institutions.
AML
Anti-Money Laundering — regulatory framework for detecting and reporting financial crime.
Confidence Score
A normalized value representing the system's certainty in a generated conclusion.
State Machine
A computational model in which the system transitions between a finite set of well-defined states.

Abbreviation Full Form
FFIRE Financial Fraud Investigation Reasoning Engine

ER Entity Relationship

A.4 Core Requirements Index (67 Requirements Catalog)
Functional Objectives (FO-1 to FO-10):
- FO-1: Accept an investigation request for a transaction or customer identifier.
- FO-2: Decompose the investigation into discrete, ordered reasoning tasks.
- FO-3: Retrieve customer, transaction, merchant, device, and location evidence in parallel.
- FO-4: Compare retrieved evidence against historical fraud patterns in the knowledge base.
- FO-5: Compute a combined risk score using rule-based and LLM-based reasoning.
- FO-6: Validate that every claim in the generated report is grounded in retrieved evidence.
- FO-7: Retry failed retrieval or validation steps up to a configurable threshold.
- FO-8: Escalate to human review when confidence falls below a configurable threshold.
- FO-9: Generate a final, structured, human-readable investigation report.
- FO-10: Log every node execution, tool call, and decision for audit purposes.

Non-Functional Requirements (NFR-1 to NFR-7):
- NFR-1: P95 investigation latency < 8 seconds for standard-complexity cases.
- NFR-2: 99.9% uptime for the API gateway and orchestration layer.
- NFR-3: Support horizontal scaling of retrieval and reasoning workers via Kubernetes.
- NFR-4: All PII encrypted at rest (AES-256) and in transit (TLS 1.2+).
- NFR-5: Every investigation must produce an immutable, timestamped audit trail.
- NFR-6: 100% of generated claims must cite a specific evidence source.
- NFR-7: Graph nodes must be independently testable and replaceable.
